summary: Defines a new DHCPv6 Unique Identifier type, DUID-UUID, derived from the standard UUID format. Devices can use their UUIDs to identify themselves to DHCP servers and vice versa, since UUIDs are globally unique and readily available on many systems.

plainLanguage.summary: Every device needs a name tag so the network address-giver recognizes it. This lets a device use its built-in one-of-a-kind ID number as that tag.

subtitle: Use a device's UUID as its DHCPv6 unique identifier.

tldr.problem: Multi-step network boot processes need a consistent identifier across firmware and boot stages, but existing DHCPv6 DUID types (link-layer, enterprise, or link-layer with timestamp) do not guarantee consistency across boot stages.
tldr.mechanism: Define a new DUID type (type 4) that embeds a Universally Unique Identifier (UUID), a 128-bit value that is often available in system firmware and inherently stable across boot stages.
tldr.outcome: Network boot can use a stable, globally unique identifier that is readily available on most modern systems without proprietary configuration.

today: RFC 6355 is a Standards Track document. DUID-UUID is now the preferred DUID type for network boot scenarios and is widely supported by modern DHCP implementations.

sections.title: The network boot challenge
sections.content: In DHCPv6, clients identify themselves to servers with a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID). When a device boots in multiple stages (firmware loads a boot loader, which loads the operating system, each stage invoking DHCP), each stage must use the same DUID so the server recognizes it is the same device and provides consistent configuration. The existing DUID types (link-layer address, enterprise number, link-layer address with timestamp) do not guarantee this consistency because the link-layer address or timestamp may differ between boot stages.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer boots, it talks to the network several times. It needs to prove it's the same computer each time, or the network server gets confused.

sections.title: DUID-UUID format
sections.content: DUID-UUID embeds a standard UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) from RFC 4122 into a DUID. The format is a 2-byte DUID-Type field with value 4, followed by the 128-bit UUID. The UUID must be persistent across system restarts, reconfiguration events, and accessible from all boot stages—typically a UUID stored in system firmware or managed by the firmware itself. This approach parallels DHCPv4 option 97, which already carries UUIDs in DHCP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: It's a 16-byte ID that the system already has built in. The network just wraps it in DHCP's format with a type number.

sections.title: UUID considerations and privacy
sections.content: The UUID must be one that remains constant and is accessible to all boot stages. UUIDs used for COM components or filesystem labels are not suitable because they may not be available to firmware or may change. DHCP traffic is sent in cleartext, so an eavesdropper can see the UUID, raising privacy concerns. However, this is not a new issue specific to DUID-UUID; all DUID types face the same limitation.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID should be permanently stored and always available. Since DHCP messages aren't secret anyway, the ID being visible is not unique to this method.

references.text: Leach, P., Mealling, M., and R. Salz, "A Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) URN Namespace", RFC 4122, July 2005.
